questions.question: A spinner is cut into 8 equal parts. 3 of the parts are red and 5 of the parts are blue. Which fraction shows the probability of the arrow landing on red?
questions.explain: The whole spinner is 8 equal parts, so the bottom number is 8 and the top number is the 3 red parts: 3/8. A common trap is writing 3/5, which compares red parts to blue parts instead of red parts to the whole spinner.

questions.question: A spinner is cut into 6 equal parts. 1 part is purple, 2 parts are green and 3 parts are yellow. Which fraction shows the probability of the arrow landing on purple?
questions.explain: Count the equal parts in the whole spinner (6) and the parts that are purple (1), so the probability is 1/6. A common trap is thinking that because there are 3 colours each colour must be 1/3 — the colours do not cover the same number of equal parts.

questions.question: A spinner is cut into 10 equal parts. 4 parts are shaded orange and the other 6 parts are white. Which fraction shows the probability of the arrow landing on an orange part?
questions.explain: The whole is all 10 equal parts and 4 of them are orange, so the probability is 4/10. A common trap is saying 1/2 because there are only two colours — the two colours do not have the same number of parts.

questions.question: A spinner is cut into 5 equal parts, labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Each part is the same size. Which fraction shows the probability of the arrow landing on the part labelled 3?
questions.explain: Only 1 of the 5 equal parts is labelled 3, so the probability is 1/5. A common trap is writing 3/5 by copying the label 3 into the top of the fraction — the top number counts the parts you want, not the number written on them.

questions.question: A fair number cube has 6 faces numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Which fraction shows the probability of rolling a 4?
questions.explain: There are 6 possible outcomes and only 1 of them is a 4, so the probability is 1/6. A common trap is saying 1/2 by thinking of it as ‘4 or not 4’ — the whole must be split into the 6 equal outcomes, not into 2 unequal groups.

questions.question: Nadia has 10 stickers in her pencil case: 2 orca stickers, 3 eagle stickers and 5 bear stickers. She pulls out one sticker without looking. Which fraction shows the probability of getting an eagle sticker?
questions.explain: The whole is all 10 stickers and 3 of them are eagles, so the probability is 3/10. A common trap is writing 3/7, which compares eagle stickers to the other stickers instead of to all 10.

questions.question: A spinner is described only by symbols: P(blue) = 3/8. Which spinner matches that probability?
options: A spinner with 3 blue sections and 8 red sections, 11 sections in all
A spinner with 8 sections that are different sizes, 3 of them blue
A spinner with 8 equal sections, 3 of them blue
A spinner with 3 equal sections, 1 of them blue
questions.explain: The bottom number 8 tells you the whole is 8 equal parts and the top number 3 tells you how many of them are blue. A common trap is choosing the spinner with 3 blue and 8 red, which reads the fraction as blue compared with red instead of blue compared with the whole.

questions.question: For a weather game, Léa uses a spinner cut into 12 equal parts: 7 parts show rain and 5 parts show sun. Which choice gives the probability of landing on sun and describes it correctly?
options: 1/2, and sun is just as likely as rain
questions.explain: Sun covers 5 of the 12 equal parts, so P(sun) = 5/12, and since 5/12 is less than half, sun is unlikely. A common trap is writing 5/7, which compares sun parts with rain parts instead of with the whole spinner.

questions.question: A spinner is cut into 8 equal parts: 4 parts are red, 3 parts are blue and 1 part is yellow. Ravi says, ‘There are 3 colours, so the probability of yellow is 1/3.’ Which statement is correct?
options: Ravi is wrong; the whole is the 8 equal parts and 1 part is yellow, so P(yellow) = 1/8
Ravi is right; with 3 colours, each colour has a probability of 1/3
Ravi is wrong; P(yellow) = 1/7 because 1 part is yellow and 7 parts are not
Ravi is wrong; P(yellow) = 3/8 because there are 3 colours out of 8 parts
questions.explain: Probability counts equal parts, not colours: 1 of the 8 equal parts is yellow, so P(yellow) = 1/8. A common trap is the one that says 1/3 — colours are only equally likely when they cover the same number of equal parts.

questions.question: Mr. Chan keeps sports cards in a jar. There are 5 hockey cards, 6 basketball cards, and 4 more soccer cards than hockey cards. One card is pulled out without looking. Which fraction shows the probability of pulling a soccer card?
questions.explain: First find the soccer cards, 5 + 4 = 9, then the whole jar, 5 + 6 + 9 = 20, so P(soccer) = 9/20. A common trap is writing 9/11, which compares soccer cards with the other cards instead of with all 20 cards.

questions.question: Maya has a spinner with 5 equal parts: 3 parts red and 2 parts white. She writes P(red) = 3/2. Which statement explains her work best?
options: Maya is right, because 3 red parts compared with 2 white parts gives 3/2
Maya should write 1/2, because the spinner either lands on red or on white
Maya compared red parts with white parts; the whole is all 5 parts, so P(red) = 3/5
Maya should write 2/5, using the 2 white parts over the 5 equal parts
questions.explain: A probability compares one outcome with the whole, so the bottom number must be the 5 equal parts: P(red) = 3/5. A common trap is 3/2, a part-to-part comparison — and a probability can never be greater than 1.

questions.question: At a Surrey rec centre, a prize spinner has 10 equal parts and 2 of them say ‘free swim’. Jayden spins and wins a free swim. Each spin is an independent event. Which fraction shows the probability that his very next spin lands on ‘free swim’?
questions.explain: Independent means the spinner does not remember the last spin, so it still has 2 winning parts out of 10 equal parts: 2/10. A common trap is 1/10, as if one win were used up — nothing is removed from a spinner.
